items.doc: Gary Burton NEA Jazz Master Oral History Interview-1
items.title: Gary Burton — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Dave Brubeck, of course, was big, so I had his records.

ctx.x: my sister would practice, watching her read the music and play the piano and so on. Then I started becoming annoying. I would yell in from the kitchen, “No, that’s supposed to be an E- flat, not an E-natural,” which she’d be in there playing, and my father would say, “wow, that’s interesting.” So he decided maybe we should start getting music lessons for Gary now. What are the choices? I remember then being taken to a few concerts or recitals, to see somebody playing the violin, and some high school band with…

that’s a C-chord, so the notes we can use are these.” Then she would say to me, “Well, now, we need an introduction or something here; make up something. And this part right here, fill in something there.” So I would have to make up something. Which was starting me to improvise. I didn’t realize it at the time. Nor did she, I’m sure. So here I am in Princeton, continuing to play the vibes and the marimba, and playing more and more gigs with a pianist-accompanist traveling with us around local schools, churches,…

Gradually finding people in Evansville that are into jazz, other kids my age in high school down there. A saxophone player and a piano player. I discovered them, that we could get together and have a jam session on a Sunday afternoon sort of thing. And I found a piano teacher. A sign suddenly outside the music store where I bought the records, saying, “Lessons In Modern Harmony.” My dad saw it first and said, “Hey, wouldn’t that be interesting for you?” So we met the guy, told him, “I’m not a piano player; I’m a…
